lessons.title: preto, branco — two blacks and a borrowed white
lessons.gloss: black and white — Portuguese has TWO blacks, and its white is a Germanic loan

segments.text: Portuguese does something the other Romance languages don't: it keeps two words for black, and the everyday one isn't the Latin one at all.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: The two blacks

utterances: word: negro. source: Latin niger. use: literary, formal, fixed phrases.
word: preto. source: Latin pressus "pressed, dense". use: the everyday colour word.

segments.text: Negro is the expected inheritance — the same niger that gave French noir and Italian nero. But day to day, Portuguese reaches for preto, from pressus ("pressed together, compact"). Dense becomes thick becomes dark: a colour named for how packed it is, not for its shade.
You already know pressus's English children: press, pressure, compress.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: branco — the Germanic import

segments.text: Latin's white, albus, lost here too. Portuguese says branco, from Germanic blank ("shining") — the same loan that gave French blanc and Italian bianco, arriving with the Suevi and Visigoths who settled Iberia.
Notice what Portuguese did to the shape: blanc- becomes branc-. The l becomes r swap is a Portuguese signature (compare plaza becomes praça, blando becomes brando).

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: Where albus went

utterances: alvorada means dawn (the sky going white).

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "o pão é branco" — Chapter 11's bread]

segments.instruction: the l becomes r swap — "blanc becomes branco"

segments.text: What are Portuguese's two blacks? (Negro from niger, literary; and preto from pressus "pressed/dense," the everyday one.) Why would "pressed" mean black? (Dense becomes thick becomes dark.) Where does branco come from? (Germanic blank, "shining" — borrowed into Romance.) What sound change shows in branco? (l becomes r, as in praça.) Next: vermelho, the strangest colour word in the language.

lessons.title: vermelho, azul — a worm and a stone
lessons.gloss: red and blue — a red named after a worm, and a blue named after a stone

segments.text: These two are the best etymologies in the whole chapter. Portuguese named its red after an insect and its blue after a rock.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: vermelho — the little worm

segments.text: Every other Romance language builds "red" on the ancient root h₁rewdʰ- (rouge, rosso, Spanish rojo, and English red, German rot). Portuguese went its own way.
vermelho from Latin vermiculus, "little worm" — the diminutive of vermis, "worm."

Why? Because the finest red dye in the ancient Mediterranean came from kermes, a scale insect harvested off oak trees and crushed for its pigment. Dyers called the creature a "little worm," and eventually the dye's name became the colour's name.
The same word gave English vermilion. And vermis gave English vermin.
Portuguese does still keep the old root — in rubro (literary "red") and ruivo ("red-haired") — but the everyday word for red is a bug.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: azul — the stone from the mountains

segments.text: azul from Arabic lāzaward from Persian lāžward: lapis lazuli, the deep-blue stone mined for millennia in Afghanistan and ground into the most expensive pigment in the medieval world.
The initial l- was lost — Spanish and Portuguese ears took it for the article l' and dropped it — leaving azul. The same journey produced French azur, Italian azzurro, and English azure.
This is the al-Andalus thread again: eight centuries of Arabic in Iberia left Portuguese and Spanish thousands of words, and one of them is a basic colour.

blocks.title: What you've built: The chapter in one table

utterances: Portuguese: vermelho. source: Latin vermiculus "little worm".
Portuguese: azul. source: Arabic lāzaward "lapis lazuli".

segments.text: Not one of Portuguese's four basic colours is a plain inherited Latin colour word.

segments.text: What does vermelho literally come from? (Vermiculus, "little worm" — the kermes insect crushed for dye.) Which English word is its sibling? (Vermilion.) Where does azul come from? (Arabic lāzaward, "lapis lazuli," via Persian — the l- lost as if an article.) What's odd about all four Portuguese colours? (None is a plain inherited Latin colour word.)
